South Africa's Growing Retail Investor Army

By: Julian Sun | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look at the staggering growth in the number of Retail Investors in South Africa

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa has seen a staggering growth in the number of retail investors over the past year. This has been amplified by the COVID-19 Pandemic. What does this growing army of Millenial Traders tell us about the state of the stock market? How long will this boom time last? Or is it a symptom of a financial bubble that will burst sooner or later?

Summary:
This story has evolved from one that looked at the phenomenon of wallstreetbets & GameStop to one that now looks at the incredible growth of retail investing in South Africa. Put simply there are hundreds of thousands of South Africans (many of them young - yesterday I spoke with a 16 year old from Bothaville for example) who are investing in the stock market.

This growth can be attributed to digital technology - there are apps like EasyEquities and El Torro that are easily downloadable onto a smartphone that make it simple to buy and trade shares on both the JSE, as well as NYSE

A second huge factor contributing to the exponential growth is the pandemic. People were stuck at home at the beginning of lockdown. Those who didn’t lose their jobs, had decreased living expenses (as a result of lockdown) and nothing to spend their disposable income on so many decided to use that money to play the stock market.


What I want to get out of this story is:

a. To showcase the exponential rise in retail investing in South Africa
b. To understand why there’s been such phenomenal growth in retail investing
c. To ask if this indicative of the euphoria associated with a financial bubble
d. To look at the consequences if the bubble bursts


Further information:
For my story I have found 2-3 really good case studies:

1. Michael Flis - Michael is a journalist and film maker who taught himself about investing during the pandemic. He has mainly invested in cryptocurrencies but has also grown a stock portfolio substantially in the past year.

2. Ryan Cherry is a 17 year old from Krugersdorp who follows R/WallstreetBets. He got caught up in the GameStop short squeeze. He bought R23000 worth of GameStop shares when they were trading at $95. He also convinced his sister (and her fiancé), his brother, mother and father to buy too. In total his family have invested R51k in GameStop shares - which they didn’t sell when the stock peaked. They still hold the stock and it’s currently trading at $46

3. Higgo van Biljon - based in Stellenbosch this 22 year old entrepreneur has grown his EasyEquities portfolio 219% in 2 years. He also runs his own app called FinMeUp - which is gives stock tips and educational information about the stock market. Higgo says that many retail investors are trading the stock market like a casino. He tells me that some subscribers to his app ask questions like: Which stocks should I buy so that I could double my money in a month? He worries that this FOMO and euphoria will end in tears when the market eventually crashes


For expert comment, I have approved economic journalist Simon Brown for comment and have also lined up CEO of EasyEqutites Charles Savage

Press Release:


Bulls & Bears, Margin Calls, Short-Selling, Cryptocurrencies, Exchange Traded Funds… The Stock Market is awash with complicated jargon that can be confusing and make us feel stupid. That’s why traditionally we’ve turned to financial advisors to help make our investment decisions. But now, thanks to the a growing army of retail investor communities online and easy-to-use apps on our smartphones, more and more South Africans are taking charge of their financial affairs like never before.

Script:


V/O: When it comes to investing, it’s easy to be intimidated by the complexities of the stock market. That’s why most people turn to financial institutions for investment advice.

But now millions around the world are using the internet to educate themselves about investing, empowering individuals to do it themselves using mobile trading apps.


V/O: Their power was on display in January when retail investors from the wallstreetbets subreddit sent the share price of American retailer Gamestop, soaring from $17 – to nearly 350 in a matter of days.

V/O: Financial Journalist Simon Brown explains what caused the Gamestop share price to skyrocket.

Simon on short interest

V/O: This is what’s known as a short squeeze. Major Wallstreet Hedge Funds had bet that the Gamestop stock would fall in price – This is called shorting the stock

But then millions of retail investors started buying Gamestop, causing the share price to rise.

To cover their losses, the Hedge Funds were forced buy the stock, sending the share price to record levels

V/O: 17 year old Ryan Cherry is a follower of Wallstreetbets who got caught up in the Gamestop euphoria

Ryan tells the story of how he came to buy Gamestop shares.

He bought R23000 worth of stock and convinced his family to invest too.

V/O: Ryan bought when Gamestop was trading at $95 but did not sell when it peaked. He watched in horror when the stock price crashed.

Comments from Ryan

LINK 1 (on couch at Digital Union): A digital revolution is fueling the staggering growth of retail investors all over the world, including South Africa. These days it’s so easy to buy shares. All you need to do is download an app onto your smartphone and you’re able to buy and sell shares from the comfort of your living room.

V/O: One of the most popular online trading apps in South Africa is EasyEquities. Charles Savage is their CEO

Charles on the background of Easy Equities

The Show & Tell with Masa illustrates just how easy it is to buy shares on his platform

V/O: The growth in retail investors has been fuelled by the COVID-19 pandemic, especially when the world first went into lockdown.

Simon Brown on why the pandemic fuelled growth of retail investors

V/O: For video editor Michael Flis, it was financial distress that motivated him.

Introduce Michael Flis as case study – Michael tells us that being in financial distress motivated him to invest in cryptocurrencies

V/O: EasyEquities also saw a surge in new subscribers

Charles Savage on the growth of EasyEquities since the start of the lockdown – have him quote the numbers

V/O: Esther Mukumbo started her account in 2018. During lockdown she had more disposable income available to invest with

Esther talks about her portfolio


V/O: Esther is one of an estimated 1 million retail investors in South Africa. But are these millennial traders responsible - with long term savings ambitions - or are they gamblers playing the stock market like a casino?

Simon on speculation



V/O: How will the growing number of South African retail investors change the way we do business?

Charles on the growth prospects for retail investing

V/O: For those considering trying their hand at retail investing, what advice should they heed?

Simon’s advice
